title: Gauging the interplay between market liquidity and funding liquidity
summary: This ECB Financial Stability Review special feature constructs composite indicators to measure market liquidity and funding liquidity in the euro area, examining how these two dimensions interact and potentially reinforce each other to generate liquidity spirals. The paper identifies three types of funding liquidity risk (rollover risk, redemption risk, and haircut/margining risk) and four dimensions of market liquidity (immediacy, breadth, depth, and tightness), noting that market liquidity is not directly observable and is complicated by data gaps for non-bank financial intermediaries.
key_points: Market liquidity and funding liquidity are inherently connected and can reinforce each other, generating liquidity spirals under stress conditions
Market liquidity has four dimensions: immediacy (pace of execution), breadth (scope of transactions), depth (size of transactions), and tightness (cost and price impact)

Funding liquidity risk manifests as three types: rollover risk (inability to replace short-term funding), redemption risk (depositor withdrawals), and haircut/margining risk (collateral valuation changes)
Market liquidity is not directly observable and existing indicators have conceptual limitations; bid-ask spreads may conceal low volume at best quotes
Bond market data is sparse due to OTC trading prevalence and waivers from transparency rules; consolidated tape providers are lacking
Cyclical factors including investor risk appetite, macroeconomic conditions, and global monetary policy cycles influence liquidity conditions
High-quality liquid asset (HQLA) holdings in banking sector have declined while bond market volatility has increased in recent periods
why_it_matters: Understanding the interplay between market liquidity and funding liquidity is essential for financial stability monitoring. When market liquidity evaporates, financial market pricing becomes less reliable and tends to overreact, leading to increased volatility and higher funding costs. This analysis helps policymakers and market participants identify conditions that could lead to systemic stress before liquidity spirals become acute.
macro_context: The paper situates liquidity analysis within the broader context of monetary policy normalisation, noting that subdued free float of high-quality debt securities combined with globally high inflation has increased bond market volatility and introduced uncertainty about future monetary policy paths.
market_structure_context: The paper discusses structural drivers of liquidity including market-making practices, issue size, trade transparency, and investor landscape. It notes data quality issues including fragmentation across commercial databases, lack of consolidated tape providers, and gaps in available data for less-regulated non-bank financial intermediaries and principal trading firms. The gradual automation of trading including high-frequency trading may undermine robustness of individual liquidity measures.
